filename: Senior Living Research Digest — Hearing Loss — October 2026.md
title: Senior Living Research Digest — Hearing Loss — October 2026
secondary_audience: families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

studies.title: Hearing Aids Didn't Prevent Dementia in a Large Trial — but Some Users' Cognitive Scores Got Better
studies.the_study: The CHOICE trial randomized 703 adults aged 60-96 (mean age 74.5) in Shanghai who had both moderate-to-severe hearing loss and mild cognitive impairment to either hearing aids or hearing care education, and followed them for 24 months. Conversion to dementia-level impairment was low in both groups and not statistically different (3.09% with hearing aids vs 4.74% with education only). However, a prespecified secondary outcome found that participants fitted with hearing aids were nearly six times more likely to improve back to a normal cognitive rating (15.3% vs 2.4%), with no study-related adverse events.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing loss is one of the most-cited modifiable dementia risk factors, and this is one of the first large randomized tests in people who already have mild cognitive impairment — the result tempers the promise of hearing aids as dementia prevention while suggesting a real, measurable cognitive benefit for some.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have both hearing trouble and memory concerns, this trial suggests hearing aids are safe and that a meaningful minority of users see their cognitive rating improve — but don't expect them to be a dementia shield. Ask your doctor about a hearing test as part of any memory workup, and treat better hearing as a quality-of-life and communication win in its own right.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living staff and family caregivers, the practical takeaway is that hearing amplification is low-risk and may help some residents re-engage cognitively; it's worth building fitting, battery checks, and daily wear support into care routines rather than marketing hearing aids as dementia prevention.
studies.caveats: The headline (primary) outcome was negative; the cognitive-improvement finding is a secondary outcome and should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Open-label design with no sham device, 24-month follow-up may be too short to detect dementia conversion, dementia conversion rates were lower than expected, participants were recruited in Shanghai and were 64% male, which may limit generalizability. Authors report multiple government research grants.

studies.title: Review of 61 Studies Finds Hearing Aids Support Brain Processing — and Earlier May Be Better
studies.the_study: Researchers systematically searched six databases for studies published between 2005 and 2025 on how hearing aid use affects thinking skills and how the brain processes sound in people with hearing loss, excluding cochlear implant users. Sixty-one papers were included. Overall, the body of evidence pointed toward hearing aid use benefiting neurocognitive function and central auditory processing, leading the authors to emphasize early rehabilitation with hearing aids.
studies.why_it_matters: Untreated hearing loss doesn't just make conversation harder — it appears to change how the brain handles sound and supports memory and attention, and this synthesis suggests waiting years to get fitted may cost more than just missed conversations.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you've been putting off a hearing test because your loss feels 'manageable,' this review argues the case for acting sooner rather than later — ask an audiologist about a baseline hearing evaluation and what a trial fitting would involve, since benefits appear tied to earlier intervention.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Families and senior living teams can use this as a prompt to normalize routine hearing screening the way vision checks are handled, and to watch for the quiet signs of untreated loss — withdrawal from group activities, TV volume creep, repeated 'what?' — rather than waiting for a resident to ask for help.
studies.caveats: Narrative systematic review with heterogeneous included studies and no meta-analysis or formal quality grading reported in the abstract; the underlying studies vary widely in design, so this cannot establish that hearing aids cause cognitive improvement. Publication bias toward positive findings is a real possibility.

studies.title: Hearing Loss Plus Multiple Health Conditions: A Risky Combination for Survival After 70
studies.the_study: Researchers at Johns Hopkins linked national survey data (NHANES 2009-2010) that included formal hearing tests with death records through 2020 for 874 US adults aged 70 and older. Over a median 9.3 years, 46% died. Sixty-five percent had measurable hearing loss, and only 27% of those used hearing aids. Hearing loss and having three or more chronic conditions each independently predicted death, but the combination carried the highest risk (adjusted hazard ratio 2.3), with a statistically significant interaction between the two.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing loss appears to amplify the danger of carrying multiple chronic conditions — plausibly because it disrupts communication with doctors, medication instructions, and self-management — yet nearly three-quarters of older adults with measured hearing loss in this sample were not using hearing aids.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are managing several chronic conditions, your hearing is part of that picture. Ask for an audiogram at your next visit, and tell your clinician directly if you miss parts of appointments or discharge instructions so they can slow down, write things down, or use an amplifier in the exam room.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care teams and senior living staff: residents with high comorbidity burden and untreated hearing loss may be the highest-risk group in your building. Consider whether hearing screening and working devices are a routine part of chronic disease management, not a separate 'ENT issue.'
studies.caveats: Observational design — it cannot show that hearing loss causes earlier death or that treating it extends life. Sample under 1,000 with wide confidence intervals (the comorbidity-alone estimate crossed 1.0). One author lists an affiliation with hearing aid company Amplifon.

studies.title: Hearing Rehab Works Online Too — Though In-Person Still Has an Edge
studies.the_study: Researchers screened 6,646 studies and pooled results from 49 (12 in meta-analyses) comparing components of aural rehabilitation — counseling, communication strategies, auditory training — delivered face to face versus through guided internet programs for adults with acquired hearing loss. In-person rehabilitation produced a medium-sized improvement in hearing-related quality of life; internet-delivered rehabilitation produced a smaller but statistically significant improvement. For broader health-related quality of life, only the internet-based programs showed a significant benefit.
studies.why_it_matters: Getting a hearing aid is only half the job; learning to use it and to manage difficult listening situations is the other half — and this review suggests that coaching delivered over the internet is a legitimate option for people who can't easily travel to a clinic.
studies.story_angle_primary: If transportation, distance or mobility keeps you from clinic visits, ask your audiologist whether a guided online aural rehabilitation program is available to you — the evidence suggests it helps, even if sitting with a clinician may help somewhat more.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living operators and family caregivers: a guided internet rehabilitation program could be delivered in-house with a staff member or family member providing the 'guided' support, extending audiology services to residents who rarely leave the building.
studies.caveats: Evidence synthesis of heterogeneous studies with varied interventions and outcome measures; only 12 of 49 studies could be pooled. Quality-of-life outcomes are self-reported by design.

studies.title: Turning Hearing Aids Down in Noisy Rooms May Make Them More Comfortable — Without Costing You Words
studies.the_study: Australia's National Acoustic Laboratories developed and tested a new hearing aid prescription setting, the NAL-NL3 Comfort in Noise Module, with 83 adult hearing aid users with mild to severe hearing loss. The module selectively reduces amplification in noisy settings by capping total loudness. Across laboratory tests and real-world smartphone-based diary assessments using different hearing aid brands, users increasingly preferred the new, quieter-in-noise setting for comfort, and lab testing found no loss in speech understanding in noise.
studies.why_it_matters: Discomfort in restaurants, dining rooms and group activities is one of the most common reasons older adults leave hearing aids in a drawer — and this suggests the fix may be a software setting rather than a new device.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your hearing aids feel harsh or overwhelming in a busy restaurant or dining room, that's a fitting problem worth raising — ask your audiologist whether your devices can be programmed with a separate, lower-gain setting for noisy environments rather than simply using the same amplification everywhere.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For communities and families: complaints that 'they're too loud' in the dining room are a legitimate, fixable fitting issue, not aid rejection or stubbornness. Noting when and where a resident removes their devices gives the audiologist exactly the information needed to adjust them.
studies.caveats: Single-site research program conducted by the developers of the fitting system, raising potential allegiance bias; partly iterative design rather than a blinded randomized trial; comfort preferences are self-reported; speech-in-noise testing was laboratory-based with short exposure.

studies.title: An Alzheimer's Drug Boosted Word Recognition in Cochlear Implant Users — In a Very Small Pilot Trial
studies.the_study: Vanderbilt researchers randomized experienced adult cochlear implant users (median age 68) to 90 days of donepezil 5 mg — a drug approved for Alzheimer's disease that boosts the brain's acetylcholine system — or placebo; 9 of 13 enrolled completed the protocol (4 donepezil, 5 placebo). Both groups wore their devices about 3 hours more per day. The donepezil group gained 14.5 points on implant-only word recognition, exceeding the 10-point threshold for clinical significance, while placebo dropped 0.8 points, and brain imaging showed increased frontal cortex activation during listening in noise.
studies.why_it_matters: It raises the possibility that a drug targeting brain plasticity could help the substantial minority of cochlear implant recipients who never achieve good speech understanding — but this is a first, exploratory signal, not a treatment.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have a cochlear implant and are disappointed with your speech understanding, the most proven lever is still the one both groups in this trial pulled: wearing the device more hours per day. Do not ask for donepezil off-label on the strength of this study — ask instead about structured auditory training and whether there are clinical trials you could join.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and audiology staff: the most reproducible finding here is that a structured 90-day protocol prompted participants to increase daily device use by about 3 hours. Encouraging and tracking consistent wear time remains the highest-yield support you can offer.
studies.caveats: Pilot trial with only 9 completers — far too small to establish efficacy or safety; single academic center; both arms also increased device use, confounding interpretation; several secondary outcomes self-reported; authors themselves state the study was underpowered.

studies.title: When Hearing Fades, the Aging Brain Appears to Lean Harder on Vision
studies.the_study: Researchers recorded brain activity with 64-channel EEG in 66 adults aged 53 to 80 with typical hearing or hearing loss while they viewed speech-like and non-speech visual stimuli. Adults with more hearing loss showed faster later-stage visual brain responses (shorter P2 latency) — a pattern consistent with the brain compensating by boosting visual processing — along with evidence that the temporal cortex, normally devoted to sound, was being recruited for visual input. The effects tracked hearing loss, not chronological age.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers biological support for something many older adults with hearing loss already do instinctively — watch faces and lips — and suggests the older brain retains meaningful adaptability that rehabilitation could deliberately exploit.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your hearing has declined, position yourself where you can see the speaker's face clearly and ask people not to talk to you from another room or while turned away — your brain is likely already recruiting vision to fill the gaps, and good lighting and sightlines give it more to work with.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and senior living design: lighting, seating arrangements that let residents see faces, and avoiding backlit or masked speakers aren't cosmetic details — they are feeding the exact compensatory channel the aging brain is using. Adjust dining room and activity room setups accordingly.
studies.caveats: Observational, cross-sectional design — cannot prove hearing loss causes the brain changes or that the changes improve real-world communication; N=66 with laboratory EEG measures rather than everyday listening outcomes; no behavioral demonstration of better lipreading or visual perception.

studies.title: Talking "clearly" helps people with hearing loss understand — but slowing down too much makes you sound robotic
studies.the_study: Twelve adult female talkers read sentences in three ways: their habitual speech, untrained "clear speech," and clear speech after a 30-minute training session. Twenty-eight normal-hearing adults then rated how natural each sample sounded on a 1-9 scale, while researchers measured speech rate, number of pauses, and pause length. Habitual speech was rated the most natural and was fastest (3.89 syllables per second); trained clear speech was rated least natural and dropped to 1.72 syllables per second with the most and longest pauses. Slower rate and more pausing strongly predicted lower naturalness ratings, revealing a trade-off between clarity and sounding natural.
studies.why_it_matters: Family members and staff are routinely told to "speak clearly" to someone with hearing loss, but this study suggests that over-coaching the technique produces exaggerated, unnatural-sounding speech that can feel patronizing — the goal is crisper articulation, not dramatic slowing.
studies.story_angle_primary: If people around you slow their speech to a crawl when talking to you, you can tell them what actually helps: facing you, enunciating, and keeping a natural rhythm rather than stretching every word. You may also want to ask your audiologist about communication-partner strategies that improve clarity without the sing-song, over-slowed delivery that many listeners find off-putting.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living staff and speech-language professionals running communication trainings, this is a caution that brief clear-speech instruction can overshoot — consider pairing training with real-time feedback on how natural the speech sounds, and note the large person-to-person variability, meaning one script will not suit every staff member or resident.
studies.caveats: Very small sample (12 talkers, all female; 28 listeners), listeners had normal hearing so intelligibility for people with hearing loss was not directly measured, laboratory sentence reading rather than real conversation, and substantial variability between both talkers and listeners.

studies.title: Struggling to hear in restaurants? Half of audiologists don't routinely test for it
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 275 licensed U.S. audiologists who perform diagnostic testing on adults about how they use speech-in-noise (SIN) testing — the measure of how well someone understands speech against background sound. Most reported high confidence in and high perceived usefulness of SIN testing, but only about half used it frequently, with usage varying sharply by workplace setting. The most common reason for testing was to validate a patient's report of difficulty hearing in noise; the most common barrier was lack of time, and testing appeared to be used more for initial assessment than for verifying how well hearing aids actually work.
studies.why_it_matters: Difficulty following conversation in noisy rooms is the complaint that most often drives older adults to seek help, yet a standard quiet-room hearing test can miss it — knowing this testing exists lets patients and families ask for it by name.
studies.story_angle_primary: If restaurants, group gatherings, or family dinners are where your hearing fails you, ask your audiologist directly for a speech-in-noise test — and ask whether it can be repeated with your hearing aids in to confirm the devices are genuinely helping in the situations that matter most to you.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and senior living professionals, this points to a concrete advocacy step at audiology appointments: because time pressure is the top barrier to this testing, requesting it in advance when booking, and asking for post-fitting verification, can make the difference between a hearing aid that sounds fine in a quiet booth and one that works in the dining room.
studies.caveats: Self-reported survey data subject to self-selection and social desirability bias — audiologists most interested in speech-in-noise testing may have been most likely to respond, so real-world usage is probably lower than reported; no patient outcomes were measured.

studies.title: Older adults with severe hearing loss show signs of an "older" immune system
studies.the_study: Researchers at a single hospital in Guangzhou, China, analyzed blood immune cell profiles in 76 older adults grouped by hearing status: normal hearing, mild-to-moderate hearing loss, or severe-to-profound hearing loss. After adjusting for age and sex, severe-to-profound hearing loss was associated with immune patterns typically seen in immune aging — a shifted T-cell balance, more differentiated CD4 cells, and higher odds of CD4/CD8 inversion. Companion analyses of publicly available mouse cochlear data pointed to inflammatory IL6/JAK/STAT3 signaling and immune-stress activity concentrated in macrophage populations.
studies.why_it_matters: It adds to evidence that significant hearing loss is not an isolated ear problem but travels with broader biological aging and inflammation — a framing that supports treating hearing as part of whole-body health in later life.
studies.story_angle_primary: There is nothing here to act on at your next appointment — no blood test for hearing loss exists — but it is a reason to treat hearing as part of your general health rather than a standalone nuisance, and to keep hearing checks on the same routine footing as vision, blood pressure, and cognition screening.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For care professionals, the practical takeaway is conceptual rather than clinical: residents with severe hearing loss may warrant attention as a group with broader health vulnerability, but these findings do not justify any new testing or intervention.
studies.caveats: Small (N=76), single-center, cross-sectional and observational — it cannot show that hearing loss causes immune aging or vice versa; the mouse transcriptomic component is from reused public data; the Chinese hospital population may not generalize; authors themselves call for validation in larger cohorts.

studies.title: Think One Ear Is Worse? You're Probably Wrong, Hearing Study Finds
studies.the_study: Researchers at a single tertiary referral center surveyed 50 adults who said their hearing was worse in one ear and who had not had a hearing test in at least five years, then compared those self-reports with formal audiometric testing. Seventy percent of patients were wrong about whether they truly had asymmetric hearing loss (defined as a 15-decibel or greater gap between ears), and 62% misidentified which ear was worse — almost always exaggerating how bad the 'bad' ear was. Misjudgment was most common among people whose overall hearing was still relatively good.
studies.why_it_matters: Asymmetric hearing loss can be a red flag for treatable or serious conditions, and it also shapes decisions about which ear gets a hearing aid — but this study shows personal impressions are an unreliable guide to what is actually happening in each ear.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have a nagging sense that one ear is weaker than the other, treat it as a reason to book a formal hearing test rather than a conclusion you can act on — and don't assume a single hearing aid in the 'bad' ear is the right answer until audiometry confirms which ear is which.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For clinicians and senior living staff: a resident's complaint of one-sided hearing trouble should trigger a referral for audiometry, not reassurance or a workaround like seating them with their 'good' ear toward the speaker.
studies.caveats: Small sample (N=50), single-center, cross-sectional design with no follow-up; patients were already seeking specialty ear care, so findings may not generalize to the broader older population.

studies.title: Nearly 6 in 10 Failed a Hearing Screening at Mobile Health Events on the Texas Border
studies.the_study: Researchers offered free hearing screenings — otoscopy, pure-tone testing and a brief case history — at six mobile health outreach events in El Paso, Texas, and analyzed results from 305 participants, 274 of them Hispanic. Fifty-seven percent failed the screening and 64% already suspected they had hearing loss. Older age, male sex, and having no insurance or public insurance rather than private coverage all predicted screening failure; primary language and neighborhood income did not.
studies.why_it_matters: It documents a large pool of undetected hearing loss in a community routinely left out of early-detection efforts, and shows that bringing screening to where people already gather can surface it — though the authors note uptake was still low and follow-up systems are the weak link.
studies.story_angle_primary: If cost or insurance has kept you from getting your hearing checked, look for free screenings at community health fairs, mobile clinics or senior centers — and if you suspect your hearing has slipped, the odds are good that you're right and worth confirming.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Community organizations and senior housing operators can use this as a template: hosting screenings is the easy part, and the study's authors stress that bilingual providers and a concrete plan for follow-up care are what turn a failed screening into actual treatment.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational; screening failure is not the same as a diagnosis; participants self-selected into health outreach events, and the single border-city population may not generalize. No data on whether anyone obtained follow-up care.

studies.title: Hospitals Stock Pocket Hearing Amplifiers — and Barely Anyone Uses Them
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted semi-structured interviews with 33 geriatricians, nurses, allied health professionals and patient-facing volunteers at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto about personal hearing amplifiers — simple assistive devices that help staff communicate with hard-of-hearing patients. Across every profession, staff described the devices as genuinely valuable but badly underused, citing three barriers: the devices were hard to find or unavailable, no one was clearly responsible for them, and they were never built into routine clinical workflow.
studies.why_it_matters: About two-thirds of hospitalized older adults have hearing loss, and missed communication in hospital contributes to confusion, poor comprehension of discharge instructions and worse outcomes — a cheap device that sits in a drawer helps no one.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're admitted to hospital, bring your hearing aids and chargers if you have them — and if you don't, ask directly whether the unit has a personal hearing amplifier you can borrow, because staff may not think to offer one.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care staff: advocate at the bedside for an amplifier during rounds and discharge teaching, and for administrators, the fix identified here is organizational — assign a role responsible for stocking, cleaning and offering the devices, and write them into admission checklists.
studies.caveats: Qualitative interviews with 33 staff at a single academic hospital; captures provider perceptions rather than patient outcomes, and no intervention was tested.

studies.title: Stem Cell Infusions Didn't Change Older Adults' Hearing — and the Study Can't Say They Would
studies.the_study: As a substudy of a nonrandomized trial of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cell infusions for vascular aging, researchers tracked hearing tests in 93 adults aged 60 to 80 (mean age 68.7) at baseline and 30, 90 and 180 days after the first infusion. Average four-frequency hearing thresholds shifted by less than 1 decibel at day 90 — smaller than normal test-retest variation — and roughly 95–97% of ears stayed within a predefined 10-decibel stability window through six months. The authors explicitly state that without an untreated comparison group, nothing can be attributed to the stem cells.
studies.why_it_matters: Stem cell clinics increasingly market anti-aging infusions, and this carefully hedged paper offers no evidence that systemic stem cells improve age-related hearing loss — a useful reality check for anyone considering paying out of pocket.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you encounter a clinic advertising stem cell therapy for age-related hearing loss, know that the best current data show essentially no change in hearing thresholds over six months — and the researchers themselves say their design can't determine whether the treatment helped at all.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families fielding questions about expensive regenerative treatments: this is a concrete example of a study whose plain-language summary admits it cannot answer the efficacy question, and a useful prompt to ask any clinic what controlled evidence exists.
studies.caveats: Single-arm exploratory substudy with no control group, nonrandomized parent trial, short six-month follow-up, and partial industry support — one author is an employee of Platinum Life Excellence Biotech (Beijing) Co., Ltd., which supported the work. Chinese population aged 60–80 selected for vascular aging criteria may not generalize.

studies.title: Training Program Brings Cochlear Implant Care Closer to Home for Veterans
studies.the_study: After a national needs assessment found too few cochlear implant-trained providers, heavy travel burdens for veterans and patchy aural rehabilitation across the Veterans Health Administration, VA clinicians built a structured mentorship program pairing experienced cochlear implant audiologists with clinicians seeking advanced training. Over two years it mentored more than 75 audiologists, expanded telehealth device programming, and supported new implant surgical and programming sites, with mentee surveys reporting gains in competency and confidence.
studies.why_it_matters: Cochlear implants are the main option when hearing aids stop helping, and geography — not candidacy — is often what keeps older veterans from getting them; expanding the trained workforce and telehealth programming shortens the drive.
studies.story_angle_primary: If hearing aids no longer give you enough benefit and you receive VA care, ask your audiologist whether you're a cochlear implant candidate and whether device programming can now be done closer to home or by telehealth rather than at a distant center.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living and care-coordination staff serving veterans: ask local VA audiology about newly added implant programming sites and telehealth options before assuming a resident can't manage the travel.
studies.caveats: Descriptive program tutorial, not a controlled study; outcomes are self-reported provider confidence and competency rather than patient hearing results; no comparison group and findings are specific to the VA system.

studies.title: Hearing Loss Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline in 10-Year Study of 6,650 Older Adults
studies.the_study: Researchers used the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey to follow 6,650 adults aged 65-99 who had at least two cognitive assessments between 2008 and 2018. Growth mixture modeling identified three cognitive paths: high-stable (83.3%), moderate decline (11.2%), and rapid decline (5.5%). Participants with hearing loss at baseline were about 26% more likely to land in the moderate-decline group and 55% more likely to land in the rapid-decline group. Notably, a strong baseline cognitive score was less protective among those with hearing loss.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing status may be a useful marker when clinicians and families assess who is at risk for steeper cognitive decline, and it is one of the few dementia risk factors that is readily detectable and potentially modifiable.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have noticed your hearing slipping, it is worth raising at your next medical appointment and asking for a hearing test — not because a hearing aid is proven to prevent decline, but because hearing status appears to be part of the bigger picture of how your brain ages, and untreated hearing loss makes everything from conversations to doctor's visits harder.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living and primary care staff: this supports folding a simple hearing screen into routine cognitive risk assessment, and recognizing that a resident with hearing loss who currently tests well cognitively may not be as low-risk as the score suggests.
studies.caveats: Observational design cannot establish causation — hearing loss may be a marker rather than a cause of decline. Hearing loss and cognition were assessed with survey measures and the MMSE rather than audiometry and full neuropsychological testing. Findings come from a Chinese cohort and may not generalize to other populations or health systems.

studies.title: How Hard You Feel You're Working to Listen Tracks With How Well You Actually Hear
studies.the_study: Researchers asked 635 participants in a longitudinal cohort spanning a wide range of ages and hearing abilities to rate their perceived performance, effort, and frustration (using a modified NASA Task Load Index) immediately after completing standard speech recognition tests. After adjusting for age, sex, and race, lower self-reported listening workload was consistently associated with better speech recognition scores — including on tests adjusted for how audible the speech actually was. In other words, the subjective sense of struggle lined up with objective listening performance beyond what volume alone explained.
studies.why_it_matters: The exhausting, frustrating feeling of straining to follow conversation is a real and measurable signal, not just a complaint — and it may help audiologists understand listening difficulties that a standard hearing test misses.
studies.story_angle_primary: If conversations leave you drained or frustrated even when you can technically hear the words, say so explicitly at your hearing appointment — your description of the effort involved carries information that the audiogram alone does not capture.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For families and care staff: a resident who withdraws from group activities or seems irritable after social time may be experiencing listening fatigue rather than disinterest or mood change, which points toward quieter settings and better room acoustics rather than less socializing.
studies.caveats: Observational and cross-sectional in its analysis — it cannot show that reducing listening effort improves speech recognition. Workload measures were entirely self-reported, and the NASA-TLX was adapted from its original aviation/workload context.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **Carryover studies, restated:** Nine items reappear from the previous digest under new headlines — "Hearing Loss Plus Multiple Health Conditions: A Risky Combination for Survival After 70" (PMID 42728658), "Review of 61 Studies Finds Hearing Aids Support Brain Processing — and Earlier May Be Better" (PMID 42447643), "Turning Hearing Aids Down in Noisy Rooms May Make Them More Comfortable" (PMID 42760273), "Older adults with severe hearing loss show signs of an 'older' immune system" (PMID 42756103), "Think One Ear Is Worse? You're Probably Wrong" (PMID 42467662), "Nearly 6 in 10 Failed a Hearing Screening at Mobile Health Events on the Texas Border" (PMID 42446280), "Hospitals Stock Pocket Hearing Amplifiers — and Barely Anyone Uses Them" (PMID 42677253), "Struggling to hear in restaurants? Half of audiologists don't routinely test for it" (PMID 42735379), "How Hard You Feel You're Working to Listen Tracks With How Well You Actually Hear" (PMID 42348455) and "Hearing Loss Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline in 10-Year Study of 6,650 Older Adults" (PMID 42753934). The access-and-delivery thread and the self-report-as-alarm thread are now firmly established rather than emerging.
- **Hearing as part of broader aging biology:** "Older adults with severe hearing loss show signs of an 'older' immune system" (PMID 42756103) and "Hearing Loss Plus Multiple Health Conditions" (PMID 42728658) continue the whole-body framing that the previous digest built with the body composition study (PMID 42717165).

**Advances**
- **From association to randomized test:** The previous digest's cognition evidence was entirely observational or synthesized — "In a 16,000-Person Cohort, People Who Said Their Hearing Was Severely Impaired Were Far More Likely to Have Dementia" (PMID 42744782), "Hearing Loss Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline" (PMID 42753934) and the 61-study review (PMID 42447643). "Hearing Aids Didn't Prevent Dementia in a Large Trial — but Some Users' Cognitive Scores Got Better" (PMID 42804222) is the first randomized test in this stream, in 703 adults who already had mild cognitive impairment.
- **Cochlear implant access widens:** "Training Program Brings Cochlear Implant Care Closer to Home for Veterans" (PMID 42418229) picks up exactly where the previous digest's "A Simple 'Hearing Stages' Conversation Tool Boosted Cochlear Implant Referrals in Hearing Aid Clinics" (PMID 42685269) stopped — the referral tool found candidates; this one addresses the shortage of trained providers and the travel burden that follow a referral.
- **Rehabilitation gets a delivery channel:** "Hearing Rehab Works Online Too — Though In-Person Still Has an Edge" (PMID 42804507) extends the access thread that previously ran through Medicaid coverage (PMID 42172530) and community screening (PMID 42446280) from finding and funding devices to the coaching that comes after them.

**Counterpoints**
- **A randomized result tempers the review:** The 61-study synthesis (PMID 42447643) emphasizes early hearing aid rehabilitation for neurocognitive benefit, and the Chinese cohort (PMID 42753934) links hearing loss to steeper decline — but the CHOICE trial's primary outcome (PMID 42804222) found no difference in conversion to dementia at 24 months. The cognitive-improvement signal was secondary and hypothesis-generating. That tension is the most important thing this run adds.
- **A null result against commercial enthusiasm:** "Stem Cell Infusions Didn't Change Older Adults' Hearing" (PMID 42819495) joins the previous digest's omega-3 null (PMID 42697173) as a second "popular remedy, no measurable hearing signal" finding — useful ballast against supplement and clinic marketing.
- **"Speak clearly" can overshoot:** "Talking 'clearly' helps people with hearing loss understand — but slowing down too much makes you sound robotic" (PMID 42757902) complicates the communication-support advice that ran through the previous digest's hospital amplifier (PMID 42677253) and listening-effort (PMID 42348455) items.

**New themes**
- **Cross-modal compensation:** "When Hearing Fades, the Aging Brain Appears to Lean Harder on Vision" (PMID 41317239) introduces a mechanism with direct environmental implications — lighting and sightlines — that no previous study in this stream touched.
- **Drug augmentation for implant users:** "An Alzheimer's Drug Boosted Word Recognition in Cochlear Implant Users" (PMID 42776967) is a new direction, though tiny.
- **Regenerative medicine enters the hearing stream:** PMID 42819495 is the first stem cell item to appear in this topic.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Across this batch, the device matters less than everything arranged around it. Hearing aids did not prevent dementia in the CHOICE trial (PMID 42804222); in the donepezil pilot, the most reproducible result was that both groups — drug and placebo — wore their implants about three hours more each day (PMID 42776967); guided internet aural rehabilitation improved quality of life (PMID 42804507); turning amplification *down* in noise made devices more comfortable without costing speech understanding (PMID 42760273); over-coached "clear speech" sounded robotic rather than clearer (PMID 42757902); and brain recordings showed older listeners leaning on vision, which makes lighting and sightlines part of the treatment (PMID 41317239).

**Why pitch this now:** A major randomized trial just landed on the modest side of the hearing-and-dementia story, and the rest of this batch quietly explains where the real, achievable gains are — wear time, coaching, fitting adjustments, and the room itself — all of which a family or a community can act on without buying anything new.

**Angle:** A reported feature that follows what should happen in the weeks and months *after* a hearing aid or implant is fitted, written for older adults and family caregivers who assumed the purchase was the finish line, with a parallel sidebar for senior living staff on dining room lighting, seating, and how to coach a care team to speak clearly without sounding patronizing.

**Potential headlines:**
- The Hearing Aid Is Only Half the Job
- Louder and Slower Are Not Always Better for Someone Who Can't Hear You
- Why the Device in Your Ear Isn't Fixing Dinner — and What Does

**Potential outlets:**
- **Next Avenue** — the gap between buying a hearing aid and actually hearing at a family dinner is exactly their blend of practical guidance and lived experience for readers over 50.
- **Senior Planet** — guided internet aural rehabilitation and programmable comfort-in-noise settings are age-tech stories for an audience that wants to understand the tools rather than just be told to use them.
- **McKnight's Senior Living** — dining room lighting, sightlines, staff communication training and fitting-review referrals are operational decisions buildings control directly.
- **Home Health Care News** — internet-delivered rehabilitation needs a "guided" human on the other end, which points squarely at home-care aides and family caregivers as an underused delivery channel.

- **Hearing Aids Didn't Prevent Dementia in a Large Trial — but Some Users' Cognitive Scores Got Better (PMID 42804222):** The careful consumer read on a headline result — hearing aids are safe and worth having, but should be sold on conversation and connection rather than as a dementia shield; for a consumer brain-health explainer or a national health news segment.
- **Review of 61 Studies Finds Hearing Aids Support Brain Processing — and Earlier May Be Better (PMID 42447643):** Pair it with the trial above as the "why waiting costs you" counterweight, reframing the decision around mental energy rather than disability; for a caregiver-advice column.
- **Hearing Loss Plus Multiple Health Conditions: A Risky Combination for Survival After 70 (PMID 42728658):** A hearing check belongs on the chronic-disease to-do list beside blood pressure and A1c — and only 27% of those with measured loss were using hearing aids; for a consumer health explainer or a care-coordination trade brief.
- **Hearing Rehab Works Online Too — Though In-Person Still Has an Edge (PMID 42804507):** For anyone who can't easily get to a clinic, what a guided online aural rehabilitation program involves and how to ask about one; for a consumer health or telehealth explainer, with a home-care operations version.
- **Turning Hearing Aids Down in Noisy Rooms May Make Them More Comfortable (PMID 42760273):** "Too loud in here" is a fixable fitting problem, not stubbornness — how to describe where and when devices come out so an audiologist can act on it; for a consumer health or age-tech column.
- **An Alzheimer's Drug Boosted Word Recognition in Cochlear Implant Users (PMID 42776967):** A restraint story — nine completers is not a treatment, and the finding anyone can use today is the three extra hours of daily device wear both groups logged; for a consumer health explainer that models how to read a tiny pilot trial.
- **When Hearing Fades, the Aging Brain Appears to Lean Harder on Vision (PMID 41317239):** Lighting, seating and facing the person you're talking to are not etiquette — they feed the channel the brain is already using; for a senior living design and activities trade piece, plus a short consumer home-setup item.
- **Talking "clearly" helps people with hearing loss understand — but slowing down too much makes you sound robotic (PMID 42757902):** A scripted "how to actually talk to someone with hearing loss" piece that corrects the well-meant slow-loud habit families fall into; for a caregiver-advice column or a staff-training trade brief.
- **Struggling to hear in restaurants? Half of audiologists don't routinely test for it (PMID 42735379):** Ask for speech-in-noise testing by name when booking, and ask again after your aids are fitted; for a consumer health explainer or an audiology practice trade brief.
- **Older adults with severe hearing loss show signs of an "older" immune system (PMID 42756103):** Handle with restraint — nothing to do differently tomorrow, but one more reason hearing belongs in routine health checks; for a short consumer science explainer.
- **Think One Ear Is Worse? You're Probably Wrong, Hearing Study Finds (PMID 42467662):** A quick, surprising service piece — trust that something changed, don't trust your guess about which ear, and don't let anyone seat you with your "good ear" forward instead of referring you; for a local-news health segment.
- **Nearly 6 in 10 Failed a Hearing Screening at Mobile Health Events on the Texas Border (PMID 42446280):** How to find a free community screening, plus an operator-facing piece on why bilingual staffing and a real referral pathway are what turn a failed screening into care; for a community-health feature and a senior-services trade piece.
- **Hospitals Stock Pocket Hearing Amplifiers — and Barely Anyone Uses Them (PMID 42677253):** Two versions — what to pack and ask for at admission, and the workflow fix of naming someone responsible for the devices; for a caregiver-advice column and a hospital or senior living operations brief.
- **Stem Cell Infusions Didn't Change Older Adults' Hearing (PMID 42819495):** A consumer-protection piece on what to ask a clinic advertising regenerative treatment for age-related hearing loss, using a study whose own authors say it cannot answer the efficacy question; for a consumer health or money-and-health section.
- **Training Program Brings Cochlear Implant Care Closer to Home for Veterans (PMID 42418229):** Veterans whose hearing aids no longer help may now have implant programming available locally or by telehealth — a concrete question to ask VA audiology; for a veterans-focused consumer outlet or a care-coordination trade brief.
- **Hearing Loss Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline in 10-Year Study of 6,650 Older Adults (PMID 42753934):** A good memory score today is less reassuring if hearing is already impaired — the case for folding a hearing screen into routine cognitive risk checks; for a consumer brain-health explainer or a senior living clinical brief.
- **How Hard You Feel You're Working to Listen Tracks With How Well You Actually Hear (PMID 42348455):** Listening fatigue is real clinical information — and a resident who withdraws after group activities may be exhausted, not disinterested; for a caregiver-advice column or senior living wellness feature.

# Fact-Check Report: Senior Living Research Digest — Hearing Loss — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-04 | **Studies reviewed:** 17
**Primary audience:** older adults and seniors | **Secondary audience:** families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

---

### Study 1: Hearing Aids Didn't Prevent Dementia in a Large Trial — but Some Users' Cognitive Scores Got Better
**PMID:** 42804222 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Caveat detail not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "dementia conversion rates were lower than expected"
- **Abstract says:** "The abstract reports conversion rates of 3.09% (intervention) vs 4.74% (control) but makes no statement about whether these were lower than anticipated."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — the claim about expected event rates may come from the full text or discussion but cannot be confirmed here.
- **Suggested fix:** "Either drop the phrase or attribute it (e.g., 'event rates in both groups were very low, limiting statistical power')."

### Study 2: Review of 61 Studies Finds Hearing Aids Support Brain Processing — and Earlier May Be Better
**PMID:** 42447643 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 3: Hearing Loss Plus Multiple Health Conditions: A Risky Combination for Survival After 70
**PMID:** 42728658 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 4: Hearing Rehab Works Online Too — Though In-Person Still Has an Edge
**PMID:** 42804507 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Named intervention components not specified in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "comparing components of aural rehabilitation — counseling, communication strategies, auditory training — delivered face to face versus through guided internet programs"
- **Abstract says:** ""This systematic review and meta-analysis compared the effects of specific components of aural rehabilitation delivered in-person and guided internet-based modalities on the quality of life (QoL) of adults with acquired hearing loss." The abstract does not name which components were studied."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only — the three listed components are plausible but not identified in the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Write 'specific components of aural rehabilitation' or attribute the list to the full text."

### Study 5: Turning Hearing Aids Down in Noisy Rooms May Make Them More Comfortable — Without Costing You Words
**PMID:** 42760273 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 6: An Alzheimer's Drug Boosted Word Recognition in Cochlear Implant Users — In a Very Small Pilot Trial
**PMID:** 42776967 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Device-use framing overstates what the trial showed** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the most proven lever is still the one both groups in this trial pulled: wearing the device more hours per day"
- **Abstract says:** ""Both groups were encouraged to increase their daily device use during the study... All study participants increased their device use, with a mean increase of 3.1 hr per day in both groups.""
- **Problem:** The trial recorded increased wear time but did not test or demonstrate that increased wear time improved outcomes; calling it 'the most proven lever' attributes evidence to this study that it does not contain.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to note that both arms increased wear time by about 3 hours daily, which confounds interpretation, and that wear-time benefit comes from other evidence, not this trial."

**Issue B. Imaging laterality omitted** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "brain imaging showed increased frontal cortex activation during listening in noise"
- **Abstract says:** ""DPZ increasing left frontal cortex activation during a speech-in-noise task (β = 3.721, p < 0.001)""
- **Problem:** The abstract specifies left frontal cortex; the digest generalizes to 'frontal cortex'.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add 'left' before frontal cortex."

### Study 7: When Hearing Fades, the Aging Brain Appears to Lean Harder on Vision
**PMID:** 41317239 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Omits counter-direction P1/N1 finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Adults with more hearing loss showed faster later-stage visual brain responses (shorter P2 latency) — a pattern consistent with the brain compensating by boosting visual processing"
- **Abstract says:** ""Participants with more hearing loss tended to have longer cortical P1 and N1 latencies in the visual evoked potential. However, the later cortical P2 response latency decreased with more hearing loss in agreement with compensatory plasticity.""
- **Problem:** The study found a mixed picture: earlier responses (P1, N1) were slower with more hearing loss, which the authors interpret as sensitivity to sensory decline rather than compensation. Reporting only the P2 result makes the compensation story look cleaner than it is.
- **Suggested fix:** "Note that earlier responses (P1, N1) were actually slower with more hearing loss, while only the later P2 response showed the compensatory pattern."

**Issue B. Temporal-cortex recruitment stimulus specificity dropped** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "along with evidence that the temporal cortex, normally devoted to sound, was being recruited for visual input"
- **Abstract says:** ""P2 responses for the non-speech stimulus showed greater cross-modal recruitment of the temporal cortex.""
- **Problem:** Cross-modal temporal recruitment was observed specifically for the non-speech stimulus, not generally — which slightly undercuts the digest's lip-reading framing.
- **Suggested fix:** "Specify that the temporal-cortex recruitment was seen for the non-speech visual stimulus."

### Study 8: Talking "clearly" helps people with hearing loss understand — but slowing down too much makes you sound robotic
**PMID:** 42757902 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline asserts an untested intelligibility benefit** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Talking "clearly" helps people with hearing loss understand — but slowing down too much makes you sound robotic"
- **Abstract says:** "The study measured perceived naturalness (rated by 28 normal-hearing adults) and acoustic variables only; intelligibility for listeners with hearing loss was not tested. The abstract refers to an "intelligibility-naturalness trade-off" as interpretation."
- **Problem:** The first half of the headline states a benefit this study did not measure; readers may assume it was demonstrated here.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe, e.g., 'Clear-speech training made talkers much slower — and listeners rated the result far less natural.'"

**Issue B. 'Patronizing' is an editorial addition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "over-coaching the technique produces exaggerated, unnatural-sounding speech that can feel patronizing"
- **Abstract says:** ""A 30-min clear speech training reduced speech naturalness compared to HS and UCS"; nothing about perceived condescension or patient reactions."
- **Problem:** Listeners rated naturalness, not how patronizing or respectful the speech felt; the inference goes beyond the data.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say the trained speech was rated markedly less natural, and note that how it is received by listeners with hearing loss was not tested."

### Study 9: Struggling to hear in restaurants? Half of audiologists don't routinely test for it
**PMID:** 42735379 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 10: Older adults with severe hearing loss show signs of an "older" immune system
**PMID:** 42756103 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 11: Think One Ear Is Worse? You're Probably Wrong, Hearing Study Finds
**PMID:** 42467662 | **Verdict:** ❌ Significant issues

**Issue A. 62% statistic misdescribed** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "62% misidentified which ear was worse — almost always exaggerating how bad the 'bad' ear was"
- **Abstract says:** "Sixty-two percent of patients misclassified the worse hearing ear, with a strong bias toward overestimation (94%). In contrast, 48% misclassified the better hearing ear, with a modest skew toward underestimation (58%)."
- **Problem:** In context (the survey quantified 'subjective individual ear hearing loss severity' for each ear), 'misclassified the worse hearing ear' means misestimating that ear's severity category, not picking the wrong ear. The digest converts a severity-estimation error into an ear-identification error, which is a different and stronger claim, and the second half of the sentence then describes severity overestimation, mixing the two.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to: '62% misjudged the severity of their worse ear, almost always overestimating how bad it was (94% of those errors), while 48% misjudged their better ear.'"

### Study 12: Nearly 6 in 10 Failed a Hearing Screening at Mobile Health Events on the Texas Border
**PMID:** 42446280 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 13: Hospitals Stock Pocket Hearing Amplifiers — and Barely Anyone Uses Them
**PMID:** 42677253 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Specific harms not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "missed communication in hospital contributes to confusion, poor comprehension of discharge instructions and worse outcomes"
- **Abstract says:** "Hearing loss is experienced by two-thirds of hospitalized older adults and is associated with poor access to healthcare and negative health outcomes."
- **Problem:** The abstract supports 'poor access to healthcare and negative health outcomes' but does not mention confusion or discharge-instruction comprehension. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Trim to the abstract's language ('poor access to care and worse health outcomes') or attribute the added detail to another source."

### Study 14: Stem Cell Infusions Didn't Change Older Adults' Hearing — and the Study Can't Say They Would
**PMID:** 42819495 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. 'Best current data' overstates a single exploratory substudy** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "know that the best current data show essentially no change in hearing thresholds over six months"
- **Abstract says:** "In this exploratory single-arm substudy, mean PTA-4 changed little over short-term follow-up... Without a concurrent audiologic comparator, the observed trajectory cannot be attributed causally to hUC-MSC administration."
- **Problem:** Calling one exploratory, single-arm, uncontrolled substudy 'the best current data' implies a broader evidence base than the abstract supports.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as 'the only published hearing data from such an infusion study — an uncontrolled substudy — showed essentially no change in thresholds over six months.'"

### Study 15: Training Program Brings Cochlear Implant Care Closer to Home for Veterans
**PMID:** 42418229 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 16: Hearing Loss Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline in 10-Year Study of 6,650 Older Adults
**PMID:** 42753934 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Interaction finding generalized** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Notably, a strong baseline cognitive score was less protective among those with hearing loss."
- **Abstract says:** "The MMSE-by-hearing interaction was significant for moderate decline (RRR 1.252, 95% CI 1.079-1.453), indicating a weaker inverse association between baseline MMSE and moderate-decline membership among participants with hearing loss."
- **Problem:** The interaction was significant only for moderate-decline membership; the digest presents it as a general effect across trajectories.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add the qualifier: 'a strong baseline cognitive score was less protective against moderate decline among those with hearing loss.'"

### Study 17: How Hard You Feel You're Working to Listen Tracks With How Well You Actually Hear
**PMID:** 42348455 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Strength of association overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "lower self-reported listening workload was consistently associated with better speech recognition scores"
- **Abstract says:** "In general, lower levels of self-reported workload were associated with better speech recognition scores, including for audibility-adjusted and non-audibility-adjusted speech recognition tasks"
- **Problem:** The abstract says 'in general,' implying the pattern did not hold uniformly across all five outcomes; 'consistently' implies it did.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'was generally associated with better speech recognition scores.'"

**Issue B. Timing of workload ratings** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "rate their perceived performance, effort, and frustration (using a modified NASA Task Load Index) immediately after completing standard speech recognition tests"
- **Abstract says:** "participants ... who completed a modified version of the ... NASA-TLX following the Northwestern University Auditory Test No. 6 (NU-6; n = 635), Speech Perception in Noise test (SPIN; n = 440), and Staggered Spondaic Word test (SSW; n = 455)"
- **Problem:** The abstract says the ratings followed each test but does not state they were taken 'immediately' after. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Drop 'immediately' and simply say the ratings were given after each speech recognition test."

## Issue Summary

| Study # | Headline | Verdict | Notes |
|---------|----------|---------|-------|
| 1 | Hearing Aids Didn't Prevent Dementia in a Large Trial — but Some Users' Cognitive Scores Got Better | ⚠️ Minor issues | Trial design, N, both outcomes and the RR of ~5.94 are reported accurately; one caveat detail (conversion rates lower than expected) isn't in the abstract. |
| 2 | Review of 61 Studies Finds Hearing Aids Support Brain Processing — and Earlier May Be Better | ✅ Accurate | Database count, date range, exclusion of cochlear implant users, 61 included papers and the authors' emphasis on early rehabilitation all match; caveats appropriately note the absence of meta-analysis and the limits on causal inference. |
| 3 | Hearing Loss Plus Multiple Health Conditions: A Risky Combination for Survival After 70 | ✅ Accurate | N=874, 46% mortality, 65% hearing loss, 27% hearing aid use, aHR 2.3 and interaction p=0.03 all match; Amplifon affiliation and the wide CI on the comorbidity-alone estimate are correctly flagged in Caveats. |
| 4 | Hearing Rehab Works Online Too — Though In-Person Still Has an Edge | ⚠️ Minor issues | Screening/inclusion numbers and both effect-size findings match the abstract; the specific rehabilitation components named are not stated in the abstract. |
| 5 | Turning Hearing Aids Down in Noisy Rooms May Make Them More Comfortable — Without Costing You Words | ✅ Accurate | Sample (83 adults, mild to severe loss), the loudness-limiting mechanism, the progressive comfort preference and the absence of detrimental effect on speech-in-noise all match; the developer-conducted, iterative, single-site nature is flagged in Caveats. |
| 6 | An Alzheimer's Drug Boosted Word Recognition in Cochlear Implant Users — In a Very Small Pilot Trial | ⚠️ Minor issues | Enrollment, completers, arm sizes, median age, 14.5 vs -0.8 point change and ~3 hr/day device-use increase all match; two small framing points about device use and the imaging finding. |
| 7 | When Hearing Fades, the Aging Brain Appears to Lean Harder on Vision | ⚠️ Minor issues | N=66, age range, 64-channel EEG, shorter P2 latency and independence from age are all accurate; the digest omits the opposite-direction P1/N1 finding and the stimulus specificity of the temporal-cortex result. |
| 8 | Talking "clearly" helps people with hearing loss understand — but slowing down too much makes you sound robotic | ⚠️ Minor issues | Talker/listener counts, rating scale, speech rates and the rate–naturalness association all match; the headline and 'Why it matters' add claims (intelligibility benefit, 'patronizing') the study did not measure, though Caveats partly cover this. |
| 9 | Struggling to hear in restaurants? Half of audiologists don't routinely test for it | ✅ Accurate | N=275, confidence/usefulness ratings, 'approximately half' frequent use, setting dependence, top reason and top barrier, and assessment-over-treatment use all match; Caveats mirror the abstract's own bias statement. |
| 10 | Older adults with severe hearing loss show signs of an "older" immune system | ✅ Accurate | N=76, single Guangzhou center, three hearing groups, age- and sex-adjusted immune findings, and the mouse bulk/snRNA-seq context are all reported accurately, with appropriately conservative framing and story angles. |
| 11 | Think One Ear Is Worse? You're Probably Wrong, Hearing Study Finds | ❌ Significant issues | Core 70% figure and sample details are right, but the 62% statistic is misdescribed: it refers to misjudging the severity of the worse ear, not misidentifying which ear is worse. |
| 12 | Nearly 6 in 10 Failed a Hearing Screening at Mobile Health Events on the Texas Border | ✅ Accurate | Sample size, setting, failure rate, suspected-loss rate and all predictors match the abstract; framing stays descriptive and caveats cover the cross-sectional design. |
| 13 | Hospitals Stock Pocket Hearing Amplifiers — and Barely Anyone Uses Them | ⚠️ Minor issues | Design, sample (33 staff, Mount Sinai Hospital, Toronto) and the three barrier themes match; one background claim in 'Why it matters' goes slightly beyond the abstract. |
| 14 | Stem Cell Infusions Didn't Change Older Adults' Hearing — and the Study Can't Say They Would | ⚠️ Minor issues | Numbers (93 participants, mean 68.7, <1 dB change at day 90, 95–97% within ±10 dB) and the authors' no-causal-attribution statement are reproduced correctly; industry support is disclosed in caveats. One phrase in a story angle overstates the evidence base. |
| 15 | Training Program Brings Cochlear Implant Care Closer to Home for Veterans | ✅ Accurate | Needs-assessment findings, >75 mentored audiologists, telehealth expansion, new sites and self-reported competency gains all match; caveats correctly identify it as a descriptive tutorial. |
| 16 | Hearing Loss Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline in 10-Year Study of 6,650 Older Adults | ⚠️ Minor issues | Cohort, N, trajectory percentages and both RRRs are accurate and framing stays associational; the interaction finding is stated more broadly than the abstract reports. |
| 17 | How Hard You Feel You're Working to Listen Tracks With How Well You Actually Hear | ⚠️ Minor issues | N=635, modified NASA-TLX domains, covariates and the audibility-adjusted finding all match; 'consistently' is slightly firmer than the abstract's hedged wording, and the timing of the ratings isn't specified in the abstract. |

**Total issues:** 14 (13 Minor, 1 Moderate, 0 Major)
